## Package Description

This is a simple feature flag service that acts as a thin frontend to the LaunchDarkly SDK. Its primary purpose is to make compliance with feature flag related NFRs much easier, since it either implements them directly or gives you an easy way to implement them. It does not create any new AWS resources, but is normally used both in the CDK code (to set up environment variables to be passed into Lambda functions) and in the Lambda code itself (to evaluate flags based on conditions).

It adds the following capabilities over using the raw LaunchDarkly SDK:
* It implements GitOps for feature flags. Thus,
  * All available feature flags are defined in a file in the git repo (`all-flags.json`) in accordance with NFR 1057.3 and 1034.5.
  * It disallows reuse of feature flags (NFR 1057.8)
  * It implements CI/CD on flags (NFR 1034.1), automatically deploying and updating them to LaunchDarkly during the deployment to the dev environment. Thus, a lot less UI work in LaunchDarkly is required. However, it does not completely eliminate it, especially once flags make it past the dev environment stage. The flags themselves are automatically promoted to all environments. However, UI interaction is required for things like adding rules, adding prerequisites, specific user targeting, etc. This is appropriate because these changes are not done as part of the flag's deployment lifecycle.
  * It does flag linting and just generally supports feature flag verification at the earliest practical development stage (NFR 1057.10 and 1034.6).
  * It automatically tags flags with the project tag and allows additional tags for jira numbers, etc.
  * It allows local overrides for default feature flag values which are applied ONLY in feature branch deployments to AWS. Through the use of a local `flags.json` file, which cannot be committed to git, a feature branch deployment can override specific flags for testing purposes in that feature branch.
  * It validates all calls to feature flags and throws an exception if a non-existent flag is used. This ensures undefined flags are always found, even in feature branch and local execution.

* It enforces naming standards for flags (NFR 1057.9), while still allowing teams flexibility in their flag naming. In other words, teams can define the format they want in the spirit of the NFR, and the service will enforce that format.
* It allows any number of base "cloneable" flags to be defined, which are then cloned for the rest of the flags. (See section on [cloning](#cloning) below.) This allows teams to do manual configuration of the cloneable flags, which will then be inherited by all other flags.
* It supports completely local operation, e.g. running Lambda code directly under nodejs.
* Flags can be used both in application logic (e.g. Lambdas) or local, CDK code. Thus the same mechanism is used to feature flag the application and the deployment code. In other words, *(Infrastructure as Code) as Code*.

Though it does not currently enforce NFR 1014.6 (monitoring of obsolete flags), the `all-flags.json` file together with flag naming standards gives us the basis to do so. We foresee building it into the lint process in the future.

In short, it does nearly everything required to support the lifecycle of feature flags following the applicable NFRs.

## Note on "environment" and "namespace" names

Many of the configuration items of this package's constructs talk about two similar-sounding and related names:
* The "environment name" (sometimes abbreviated as `envName`), which refers to a specific deployment of the Reference Architecture application in AWS.
* The "namespace", which refers to a level of deployments of the Reference Architecture application.

For most Reference Architecture applications, there are four "namespaces":
* `dev`, which is used by the development team for development purposes
* `int`, which is used primarily by the QA team, and is the primary place where QA testing is done
* `stgus`, which is also used primarily by the QA team, it is where all the applications can be seen together in one place, and we can test for (probably unwanted) interactions between them.
* `produs`, which is the production system seen by customers.

For anything past `dev`, the "namespace" is always the same as the "environment name". In `dev`, there are two options:
* The application's main branch is always deployed directly into the fixed `dev` environment. Like the other namespace/environments, there is only one `dev`.
* Developers can do personal or "feature branch" deployments to other environment names, all of which come under the `dev` namespace. Because we are following GitOps processes, the feature branch environment names are by convention the same as the git branch name, and always are prefixed by `dev/` since they are in the `dev` namespace. So a branch name might be `dev/ESP-1234`, which deploys into the `dev/ESP-1234` environment name (which is in the `dev` namespace).

# Usage


## CI/CD

In our pipeline, we will be using the below command to create the feature flags.

```typescript
    npx deploy-feature-flags --apikey $LD_API_KEY
```
By default it will use the `dev` environment to deploy the feature flag.
But if you have any other environment for development like example - Bronze

You can use the below command
```typescript
    npx deploy-feature-flags --apikey $LD_API_KEY --env bronze
```

## Examples

Here's an example of using the package. In your CDK code:

```typescript
    const flags = new FeatureFlags(this, 'feature flags', {
      namespace,
      envName,
      defaultLambdaVars: appStackProps.lambdaVars
    });
```

In your Lambda code:

```typescript
  const myFlagValue = await getBoolean(name: string, defaultValue?: boolean);
```

You can also pass in some additional custom "user" attributes. This lets you specify things like district-specific flags.

```typescript
  const myFlagValue = await getBoolean(name: string, {
    defaultValue: true,
    user: {
      custom: {
        district_uid
      }
    }
  });
```

## Configuration

The definition of the `getBoolean` function is:

```typescript
/**
 * Get a boolean feature flag value. This is the main entry point for Lambda functions.
 * @param name full name of feature flag (see NFR)
 * @param defaultValue optional default value of flag; defaults to false
 * @returns Promise to get the feature flag value
 */
export async function getBoolean(name: string, defaultValue?: boolean): Promise<boolean> {
  ...
}
```

The following properties are most commonly used on the [`FeatureFlags`](./classes/FeatureFlags.html) construct:

|Key|Type|Meaning|
|---|----|-------|
|`environmentName`|string|The "environment name" (see note above).|
|`namespace`|string|The "namespace" (see note above).|
|`lambdaVars`|`Record<string,string>`|Common environment variables to be combined with variables set in the construct.|

## Useful public members

The CDK construct exposes the following useful public members:

* `lambdaVars`: Set of environment variables to be passed to all Lambda functions. These configure the runtime feature flag code.

## Flag Cloning

All normal feature flags are cloned from one or more "cloneable" flags. The idea is the cloneable flags allow you to do external, currently manual, configuration of the cloneable flags, and all future flags created from them get those same attributes. As noted above, this library is really only a thin layer on top of LaunchDarkly for CI/CD and to help with NFR compliance and so "cloning" directly uses the normal LaunchDarkly ["create flag as a clone" operation](https://launchdarkly.com/blog/launched-clone-flags/]).

The above link explains how LaunchDarkly foresees using clones, but the idea here is a project can define a set of base flags and then have new flags inherit attributes from them. Unfortunately (or maybe fortunately), any changes to the base flag do not propagate to flags previously cloned from it. In truth, either way there could be problems, so we just directly inherit LaunchDarkly's cloning behavior.

"Cloneable" flags are really just regular feature flags in LaunchDarkly, but this library implements a few things:

* They have "clone" as their flag type, which strictly speaking is not specified in the NFR
* They are NOT specified as regular flags in the `flags` section of `all-flags.json`, but as `clone` properties. They are automatically generated as needed by the library's CI/CD function.
* They are specified as ["permanent" flags in LaunchDarkly](https://docs.launchdarkly.com/home/flags/settings).

As noted above, you can specify multiple cloneable flags for a project, but this is not expected to be common. Most likely a single top-level `clone` property/flag will be sufficient for most projects.

## Local-only flags

Local-only flags allow setting values on your local workstation and in feature branch deployments, but are never "promoted" up to LaunchDarkly. This means they can never be enabled in a fixed environment such as dev, qa, or prod.

Local-only flags:

* Can be identified by having a type of "local" (e.g. pscc-local-20220508-something)
* Are set by adding a value to the local `flags.json` file
* Are always valid, and always - except in feature branches - return false (thus a default-true local flag is not possible)
* Cannot be put in all-flags.json, so they can never be created in LaunchDarkly

## Flag files

All feature flag files are located in the `resources/feature-flag` folder of the root directory. There are two flag files, one required and the other optional.

### File: all-flags.json

`all-flags.json` is always required when using flags. It defines the universe of possible flag values and drives the flag CI/CD. Here is a typical file:

```
{
  "deploy": true,
	"project_key": "ps-compliance-cloud",
	"flag_format": "pscc-<type>-<date>-<description>",
	"project_tag": "pscc",
	"clone": "pscc-clone-20220505-basic",
	"flags": {
		"pscc-release-20220317-faster-step-function-deploy": {
			"description": "this is actually a deploy-time flag",
			"name": "pscc-release-20220317-faster-step-function-deploy",
			"tags": [ "CAP-38" ]
		},
		"pscc-release-20220505-manage-test13": {
			"tags": [ "CAP-38", "BOGOSITY" ],
			"clone": "pscc-clone-20220505-basic-test"
		}
	}
}
```

The top-level keys are as follows:

| Key         | Default   | Description  |
|-------------|-----------|--------------|
| deploy      | false | Whether to use feature flags. This must be set to `true` to use any of the `@ps-refarch/feature-flags` functionality. |
| project_key | N/A | Your project's key in LaunchDarkly. It appears in every URL. |
| flag_format | N/A | The flag format all flag keys must use, which enforces naming consistency. This is basically a regular expression, with some placeholders that make it easier to meet the NFR. The placeholders are `<type>` (one of the feature flag types defined in the NFR), `date` (a date in the recommended YYYYMMDD format), and `<description>` (basically `/.*/`). You MUST use `<type>` somewhere in there. |
| project_tag | N/A | The project tag to be applied in LaunchDarkly, usually a short abbreviation of the project like `PSCC` or `UV`. |
| clone       | N/A | The default flag key to clone for all newly-created flags. If the flag does not yet exist, it is created with a simple default configuration. |

The flag-level object key is the name of the flag, which needs to meet the `flag_format` for the file. The flag-level keys are (in more or less order of importance):

| Key         | Default   | Description  |
|-------------|-----------|--------------|
| tags        | N/A       | Additional tags to define. Usually the jira epic number is used, plus others if you want. If you have multiple teams using the same project in Launch Darkly, it would be useful to give each team its own tag to make finding their flags easier. |
| name        | flag key  | The flag’s name. If not specified, it uses the key. We recommend you definitely not think too hard about this. If a good name comes to mind, use it; otherwise, just omit it and the flag's key will be used. It really doesn't make any sense to spend a lot of brain power coming up with a name just for the sake of doing it: "replace dashes with spaces" is not really a worthwhile algorithm. Again, you can always update it later if you get inspired. |
| description | Empty     | Text description for the flag. Teams should carefully consider what to put in the flag's description, since this will be very useful for a flag you defined months or years previous. One key part of this description should be `WHEN ON: <Describe exactly what the flag does>`. It is very likely that this will not be obvious from the description in the flag's key. Since flipping the flag in production will have impact on potentially thousands of end users, we should understand exactly what flipping that flag will do. |
| clone       | top-level clone flag | The flag to clone. The top-level `clone` property is used as a default, so 95% of the time you can just omit it. |
| default     | false      | The flag's default value. There really isn't a lot of good reason that we can think of to change this from the default, so leave it out. |

### File: flags.json

Unlike `all-flags.json`, the `flags.json` file is optional. Its purpose is to override default flag values for local execution and feature branch deployments ONLY. It has a very simple format exemplified by:

```
{
    "pscc-release-20220317-faster-step-function-deploy": true
}
```

It's simply name/value pairs that override the default values specified in `all-flags.json`. All flags 
This file is read locally and deployed to Lambdas in feature branch deployments into AWS.

## Lifecycle of a Feature Flag, GitOps style

As noted above, this service brings a consistent GitOps based lifecycle to feature flags. This section outlines how to add a new feature flag to the system.

1. Decide which existing cloneable flag you want the new flag to clone. The `all-flags.json` file defines a default cloneable flag, which is sufficient for 95% of the use cases, so most of the time you don't even have to worry about this part.
2. Decide what key you are going to give your flag. The key needs to meet your project's naming standard (set up at the beginning of the project, but which should roughly meet NFR 1057.9). A typical flag name would be `pscc-release-20220505-my-cool-feature`. Make sure it's all in lower-case, since the service enforces that.
3. Decide what tags you want the flag to have. You don't have to include the project tag, as that will be included automatically. Typically the jira epic number is used, but you can use as many as you want.
4. Decide if you want to give a name and description to the flag. The name and description aren't used for anything important, but they do show up in the LaunchDarkly UI, so you should use something that makes sense. If you can't think of a good specific name, just leave it undefined and the service will use the flag's key. Description is also optional, but we recommend creating one by thinking about the uses of the flag, its probably lifetime, and anything else a flag user needs to know.
5. Add your new flag to `all-flags.json` in the `flags` section. The only required field in that section is `tags` (which can be an empty array).
6. Run flag lint to make sure there are no problems with `all-flags.json`. From the root application directory, run `yarn lint-feature-flags`.

## Setting up a new project

### External Configuration

* Get SDK keys for each fixed env (dev, qa, prod) from LaunchDarkly. The SDK key is read-only and used for normal feature flag operations.
* Get an API key to run CI/CD. Apparently we don't have privileges to create a service key, so somebody will have to create a personal API key. This needs to be able to read and write to the API.
* Put the API key in a secret string-type SSM parameter `/launch-darkly/api-key` in the tooling account. Something like this:

```
# NOTE: First need to set AWS credentials for tooling account
aws ssm put-parameter --name '/launch-darkly/api-key' --region us-east-1 --type SecretString --value 'api-XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX'
```

* Put the SDK keys into SSM Parameters `/launch-darkly/<envNamespace>/key` as string type (not secret string, as this is not particularly sensitive). Note this is one per environment *namespace*, not strictly one per environment. This means all feature branch environments (e.g. `dev/PSSR-123456`) use the same `dev` key since they are all in the `dev` namespace as indicated by the git branch name. Note that, unlike the API keys which are put in the tools account, the SDK keys are put into the deployment accounts (preprod/prod).

```
# NOTE: First need to set AWS credentials for pre-prod account
aws ssm put-parameter --name '/launch-darkly/dev/key' --region us-east-1 --type String --value 'sdk-XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX'
aws ssm put-parameter --name '/launch-darkly/int/key' --region us-east-1 --type String --value 'sdk-XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX'
aws ssm put-parameter --name '/launch-darkly/stgus/key' --region us-east-1 --type String --value 'sdk-XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX'

# NOTE: First need to set AWS credentials for prod account
aws ssm put-parameter --name '/launch-darkly/produs/key' --region us-east-1 --type String --value 'sdk-XXXXXXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXXXXXXXXXX'
```

### Internal Configuration

* Decide on what you want to call your base cloned flag. We recommend something like `pscc-clone-20220505-base` (substitute your project and date). You can create/update this flag yourself in LaunchDarkly, or you can let the library auto-create it. Either way, you can go into the portal and tweak it yourself later.
* Create `all-flags.json` as described above with the information you got above
* Run flag lint to make sure there are no problems with `all-flags.json`. From the root application directory, run `yarn lint-feature-flags`.

NOTE: We should maybe update the account/region repo documentation to explain creating the API key parameter in SSM, or do it automatically via CDK.

## NPM Authentication

This package assumes you have your `~/.npmrc` set up as described in [the root README of this project](https://gitlab.com/powerschoolgroup/reference-architecture-templates/blueprint-package). Otherwise, you will not be able to do the necessary `yarn install` for this package.
